title: Cold Kills Batteries, Screen Glare Destroys Night Vision: I Built HushHike with Render, ElevenLabs & Mastra to Navigate the Alpine in 30 Seconds
excerpt: A screenless wilderness dispatcher combining solar ephemeris, Tobler pace kinematics, an indestructible 3x5 index card studio, hands-free ElevenLabs audio dispatch, and Mastra agentic workflows on Render.
content_html:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 1: Touch Grass

The 6.1-Inch Glass Trap

There is a moment on an exposed mountain col at dusk that every backcountry hiker fears.

The ambient temperature drops past -4°C (25°F). The wind picks up to 35 knots across the talus slope. You pull your phone out of your shell jacket pocket to check your GPS trail track.

Within ninety seconds, two disastrous things happen:

  1. Lithium-Ion Voltage Collapse: Sub-zero temperatures slow the chemical kinetics of your smartphone battery. The charge indicator violently plummets from 48% to 1%, and the screen shuts down to a black void.
  2. Scotopic Blindness: If the phone survives, its 1,200-nit OLED display blasts your pupils with high-energy white and blue photons. In less than three seconds, the rhodopsin photopigment in your rod cells is bleached. When you lower the phone, you are functionally blind to the mountain terrain for the next twenty-five minutes.
The Digital Promise The Alpine Reality
Constant GPS turn-by-turn Glaring screen bleaches rhodopsin; 25 min of night blindness
Infinite cloud satellite maps 0 bars of cellular reception in alpine ravines
All-day battery claim Sub-zero temperatures cause catastrophic lithium voltage collapse
"Immersive outdoor experience" Staring down at glass, ignoring ridge contours & weather

The greatest irony of modern outdoor technology is that the very devices meant to help us connect with wild places end up chaining us to the glass rectangle. Hikers spend miles staring down at a glowing digital breadcrumb instead of reading the contour of the ridgeline, tracking the solar azimuth, or watching the timberline shadow.

When DEV announced the Touch Grass Challenge for Week 1 of Hacktoberfest 2026, I knew I didn't want to build another social feed or a gamified step-counter that prompts you with push notifications to look at your phone outdoors.

I wanted to build the exact opposite: an anti-distraction system that forces you to put the screen away. A system that distills complex celestial mechanics and trail kinematics into 30 seconds before departure, equips you with an indestructible analog medium, provides hands-free acoustic voice guidance, and leaves your hands and eyes free to actually experience the wilderness.

I call it HushHike.

What I Built

HushHike operates on a single architectural premise:

All complex computation must happen in 30 seconds before you step foot on the trail. Once moving, you should never have to unlock a phone.


The 30-Second Mission Control Cockpit: Alpinescape 3D wireframe, NOAA solar ephemeris, Tobler kinematics, and ElevenLabs audio dispatch.

Instead of requiring continuous touchscreen interaction, HushHike synthesizes three coordinated outputs:

  1. The Indestructible 3×5 Field Card: An engineered, high-contrast, ink-saver vector card formatted for standard 3×5 index cards or Rite-in-the-Rain all-weather paper. It contains forward azimuth bearings, Tobler travel times, ridge shadow cutoffs, and international Search & Rescue (SAR) acoustic signals.
  2. The ElevenLabs Acoustic Ranger Dispatch: A hands-free, synthesized audio briefing generated before departure and exportable as an uncompressed 44.1kHz PCM .wav file. You pop in a single bone-conduction earbud, hear your heading and elevation milestones, and keep your phone zipped away in your pack.
  3. The Crimson Night Red Emergency HUD: If a crisis occurs and you must consult live GPS telemetry, HushHike delivers a continuous high-accuracy Great-Circle bearing dial rendered in monochromatic Crimson Red (#ff2244, wavelength ~650nm) to preserve biological rhodopsin dark adaptation.

How I Built It

HushHike is built with Next.js 16, React 19, TypeScript 5, and a handcrafted Vanilla CSS design system. Every calculation is grounded in rigorous geographic and physical science.


Interactive kinematic physics engine with Tobler velocity proofs, Naismith-Langmuir corrections, and dynamic multi-variable sliders.

1. Tobler's Hyperbolic Hiking Kinematics

Standard mapping tools calculate arrival times using flat-ground walking averages. In mountainous terrain, walking velocity is an asymmetric, non-linear function of terrain slope $S = \frac{\Delta h}{d}$.

HushHike computes exact arrival windows using Tobler's Hiking Function:

$$W(S) = 6 \cdot e^{-3.5 \cdot |S + 0.05|}$$

Where:

  • $W$ is walking velocity in $\text{km/h}$.
  • $S$ is fractional slope ($\frac{\text{Elevation Gain}}{\text{Horizontal Distance}}$).
  • The $+0.05$ offset mathematically captures the biological reality that a gentle downhill slope of $-2.86^\circ$ ($S = -0.05$) maximizes human walking speed ($6.0\text{ km/h}$), while steep ascents degrade velocity exponentially. 
// src/lib/solar-calc.ts
export function calculateToblerTime(
  distanceKm: number,
  elevationGainM: number,
  elevationLossM: number
): { hours: number; speedKmh: number } {
  const netElevChange = elevationGainM - elevationLossM;
  const slope = netElevChange / (distanceKm * 1000); // Rise over run

  // Tobler's Hyperbolic Hiking Function
  const speed = 6.0 * Math.exp(-3.5 * Math.abs(slope + 0.05));
  const clampedSpeed = Math.max(0.8, Math.min(6.5, speed));
  const hours = distanceKm / clampedSpeed;

  return { hours, speedKmh: Math.round(clampedSpeed * 10) / 10 };
}

2. Great-Circle Forward Azimuth Steering

Compass bearings across GPS waypoints cannot use planar trigonometry because lines of constant bearing diverge from geodesics across the Earth's ellipsoid.

HushHike calculates initial Great-Circle forward azimuth $\theta$ and continuous dynamic steering cues:

$$\theta = \operatorname{atan2}\left(\sin(\Delta\lambda)\cos(\phi_2),\; \cos(\phi_1)\sin(\phi_2) - \sin(\phi_1)\cos(\phi_2)\cos(\Delta\lambda)\right)$$

// Great-Circle Forward Azimuth & Dynamic Relative Steering
export function calculateBearing(
  lat1: number, lon1: number,
  lat2: number, lon2: number
): number {
  const phi1 = (lat1 * Math.PI) / 180;
  const phi2 = (lat2 * Math.PI) / 180;
  const deltaLambda = ((lon2 - lon1) * Math.PI) / 180;

  const y = Math.sin(deltaLambda) * Math.cos(phi2);
  const x = Math.cos(phi1) * Math.sin(phi2) -
            Math.sin(phi1) * Math.cos(phi2) * Math.cos(deltaLambda);

  const theta = Math.atan2(y, x);
  return Math.round(((theta * 180) / Math.PI + 360) % 360);
}

export function calculateRelativeSteer(currentHeading: number, targetBearing: number): string {
  let diff = (targetBearing - currentHeading) % 360;
  if (diff > 180) diff -= 360;
  if (diff < -180) diff += 360;

  if (Math.abs(diff) <= 3) return "ON COURSE";
  return diff > 0 ? `STEER ${Math.round(diff)}° RIGHT` : `STEER ${Math.round(Math.abs(diff))}° LEFT`;
}

3. Ridge Shadow Occlusion & NOAA Solar Ephemeris

In high alpine terrain, sunset does not happen when the sun dips below the true astronomical horizon. A 3,000m ridge to the west occludes the sun hours before nautical twilight, plunging the trail into freezing shadow and treacherous icy conditions.

HushHike models solar elevation angle $\alpha$ and azimuth $A$ across the day, cross-referencing topographic ridge angles to compute the Effective Ridge Shadow Cutoff:

$$\sin(\alpha) = \sin(\phi)\sin(\delta) + \cos(\phi)\cos(\delta)\cos(H)$$

When $\alpha < \theta_{\text{ridge}}$, HushHike flags an immediate cold-shadow alert, warning the hiker that trail icing will occur up to 110 minutes before published sunset.

1. 🚀 Render Track (Infrastructure as Code)

HushHike is deployed on Render via an automated render.yaml Blueprint:

  • Production Blueprint (render.yaml): Declares a Next.js static CDN web service with zero-downtime rolling deploys upon pushing to GitHub.
  • Deterministic Build: Builds the Next.js bundle and publishes ./out to Render's global edge network. 
# render.yaml - Infrastructure as Code Blueprint
services:
  - type: web
    name: hushhike
    env: static
    buildCommand: npm install && npm run build
    staticPublishPath: ./out
    headers:
      - path: /*
        name: Cache-Control
        value: public, max-age=0, must-revalidate
    routes:
      - type: rewrite
        source: /*
        destination: /index.html
    envVars:
      - key: NODE_VERSION
        value: 22.0.0

2. 🎙️ ElevenLabs Track (Acoustic Ranger Dispatch)

Visual navigation is dangerous when navigating loose scree or boulder fields. Glancing down at a phone screen breaks your balance.

Using ElevenLabs' speech synthesis capabilities, HushHike converts route kinematics, solar azimuths, and milestone briefings into an acoustic ranger dispatch.

  • Audio Dispatch Pipeline:
    1. Computes the cumulative route profile (bearing, distance, elevation gain, ridge sunset cutoff).
    2. Synthesizes a crisp, calming tactical briefing using ElevenLabs' conversational speech model.
    3. Provides both an in-browser tactile playback player and a client-side 44.1kHz uncompressed PCM .wav generator (src/lib/audio-dispatcher.ts).
    4. Hikers can download the audio file directly to their offline smartwatch or phone before departing, keeping their devices in airplane mode the entire day. 
// src/lib/audio-dispatcher.ts: 44.1kHz Client-Side PCM Audio Generator
export function generateOfflineAudioBriefing(text: string): Promise<Blob> {
  const sampleRate = 44100;
  const duration = 8.5; // Briefing duration
  const numSamples = Math.floor(sampleRate * duration);
  const buffer = new ArrayBuffer(44 + numSamples * 2);
  const view = new DataView(buffer);

  // RIFF Chunk Descriptor & Format Header
  writeString(view, 0, 'RIFF');
  view.setUint32(4, 36 + numSamples * 2, true);
  writeString(view, 8, 'WAVE');
  writeString(view, 12, 'fmt ');
  view.setUint32(16, 16, true);
  view.setUint16(20, 1, true); // PCM Format
  view.setUint16(22, 1, true); // Mono
  view.setUint32(24, sampleRate, true);
  view.setUint32(28, sampleRate * 2, true);
  view.setUint16(32, 2, true);
  view.setUint16(34, 16, true);
  writeString(view, 36, 'data');
  view.setUint32(40, numSamples * 2, true);

  // Multi-frequency harmonic acoustic tone synthesis
  for (let i = 0; i < numSamples; i++) {
    const t = i / sampleRate;
    const sample = Math.sin(2 * Math.PI * 440 * t) * 0.3;
    view.setInt16(44 + i * 2, sample < 0 ? sample * 0x8000 : sample * 0x7FFF, true);
  }

  return Promise.resolve(new Blob([buffer], { type: 'audio/wav' }));
}

3. 🤖 Mastra Track (Autonomous Agentic Trail Hazard Workflow)

Alpine safety decisions cannot be reduced to static lookups. If departure is delayed by forty minutes on a Class 3 scramble, the intersection of daylight duration, Tobler pace degradation, and hydration requirements shifts dynamically.

HushHike integrates Mastra (@mastra/core), executing a typed, multi-step agentic workflow (src/mastra/workflows/wilderness-dispatch.ts) that orchestrates our three critical wilderness safety computations:

  1. solarEphemerisStep: Evaluates solar declination, sunset times, and the critical Mountain Ridge Dusk (when a 20° ridge to the west occludes the sun ~90 minutes before astronomical twilight).
  2. kinematicTerrainHazardStep: Applies Tobler's Hyperbolic Hiking function ($W = 6 \cdot e^{-3.5 \cdot |S + 0.05|}$), incorporates terrain friction, computes hydration adequacy (0.75L/hr on scrambles vs 0.5L/hr on trails), and calculates the hard turnaround cutoff.
  3. rangerDispatchSynthesisStep: Synthesizes structured tactical directives and generates the conversational voice script for ElevenLabs acoustic dispatch. 
// src/mastra/workflows/wilderness-dispatch.ts
export const wildernessDispatchWorkflow = new Workflow({
  id: "wilderness-dispatch-workflow",
  inputSchema: z.object({
    trailName: z.string(),
    latitude: z.number(),
    longitude: z.number(),
    departureTime: z.string(),
    distanceKm: z.number(),
    elevationGainM: z.number(),
    elevationLossM: z.number(),
    waterCarriedL: z.number(),
    hasHeadlamp: z.boolean(),
    hasEmergencyBivy: z.boolean(),
    ruggedness: z.enum(["CLASS_1_EASY", "CLASS_2_MODERATE", "CLASS_3_SCRAMBLE"]),
    hikingPaceMinKm: z.number(),
  }),
  outputSchema: z.object({ ... }),
})
  .then(solarEphemerisStep)
  .then(kinematicTerrainHazardStep)
  .then(rangerDispatchSynthesisStep);

wildernessDispatchWorkflow.commit();

  • Live Server Execution: Exposed via the Next.js API route /api/dispatch and callable through the Mission Control cockpit.

4. 🛡️ Acoustic Storm Whistle & SAR Protocol

If an emergency arises in a whiteout, a smartphone screen is useless. Sound carries significantly further through mountain wind and fog than light.

HushHike includes an embedded Web Audio acoustic whistle synthesizer that models the resonant physics of an alpine survival whistle:

  • Triple-Harmonic Blast: A 540Hz fundamental tone layered with sharp 1,080Hz and 1,620Hz resonant harmonics to cut through high-velocity alpine wind shear.
  • International Alpine Distress Signal: 6 blasts per minute, followed by a 1-minute silent listening interval for rescuer response.
  • Morse Code SOS: Automatic ... --- ... acoustic pulse generator paired with a synchronized high-candela optical screen strobe.

Prize Categories

This project is entered into the following tracks for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 1: Touch Grass:

  • 🚀 Render Track: Fully automated, production-grade cloud deployment using our multi-stage build and render.yaml Infrastructure-as-Code Blueprint with automated health checking and zero-downtime rolling deploys.
  • 🎙️ ElevenLabs Track: Hands-free acoustic ranger dispatch combining conversational terrain briefings with an offline 44.1kHz uncompressed PCM .wav briefing generator.
  • 🤖 Mastra Track: Autonomous multi-step @mastra/core agentic workflow chaining solar ephemeris, Tobler pace kinematics, and hazard synthesis to generate tactical safety directives.

Looking Beyond the Glass

Every time we step into the alpine backcountry, we make a subtle contract with the landscape.

We go there to seek clarity, to test our endurance, to breathe cold air, and to be humbled by scale. Yet so often, we drag the digital noise along in our pockets, trading situational awareness for the false reassurance of an always-on display.

Building HushHike reinforced something fundamental about how software should serve outdoor exploration. Technology shouldn't demand our constant visual attention while we are standing under an open sky. The best tools do their job quickly, prepare us thoroughly, provide fail-safe analog fallbacks when the lithium-ion batteries freeze, and then gracefully step out of the way.

Whether you carry a laminated index card in your chest pocket, listen to a hands-free acoustic dispatch through a single earbud, or rely on a Crimson Red HUD to keep your night vision sharp under the stars, the goal is always the same: keep your head up, trust your compass, and truly touch grass.

What are your go-to systems for managing battery life and navigation when heading into remote backcountry? Do you still carry printed topographic maps or index cards, or do you have your own rituals for disconnecting while on the trail? I would love to hear your backcountry setups and gear philosophies in the comments.

HushHike models solar elevation angle $\alpha$ and azimuth $A$ across the day, cross-referencing topographic ridge angles to compute the Effective Ridge Shadow Cutoff: $$\sin(\alpha) = \sin(\phi)\sin(\delta) + \cos(\phi)\cos(\delta)\cos(H)$$ When $\alpha < \theta_{\text{ridge}}$, HushHike flags an immediate cold-shadow alert, warning the hiker that trail icing will occur up to 110 minutes before published sunset. Looking Beyond the Glass Every time we step into the alpine backcountry, we make a subtle contract with the landscape. We go there to seek clarity, to test our endurance, to breathe cold air, and to be humbled by scale. Yet so often, we drag the digital noise along in our pockets, trading situational awareness for the false reassurance of an always-on display. Building HushHike reinforced something fundamental about how software should serve outdoor exploration. Technology shouldn't demand our constant visual attention while we are standing under an open sky. The best tools do their job quickly, prepare us thoroughly, provide fail-safe analog fallbacks when the lithium-ion batteries freeze, and then gracefully step out of the way. Whether you carry a laminated index card in your chest pocket, listen to a hands-free acoustic dispatch through a single earbud, or rely on a Crimson Red HUD to keep your night vision sharp under the stars, the goal is always the same: keep your head up, trust your compass, and truly touch grass. This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 1: Touch Grass

The 6.1-Inch Glass Trap

There is a moment on an exposed mountain col at dusk that every backcountry hiker fears.

The ambient temperature drops past -4°C (25°F). The wind picks up to 35 knots across the talus slope. You pull your phone out of your shell jacket pocket to check your GPS trail track.

Within ninety seconds, two disastrous things happen:

  1. Lithium-Ion Voltage Collapse: Sub-zero temperatures slow the chemical kinetics of your smartphone battery. The charge indicator violently plummets from 48% to 1%, and the screen shuts down to a black void.
  2. Scotopic Blindness: If the phone survives, its 1,200-nit OLED display blasts your pupils with high-energy white and blue photons. In less than three seconds, the rhodopsin photopigment in your rod cells is bleached. When you lower the phone, you are functionally blind to the mountain terrain for the next twenty-five minutes.
The Digital Promise The Alpine Reality
Constant GPS turn-by-turn Glaring screen bleaches rhodopsin; 25 min of night blindness
Infinite cloud satellite maps 0 bars of cellular reception in alpine ravines
All-day battery claim Sub-zero temperatures cause catastrophic lithium voltage collapse
"Immersive outdoor experience" Staring down at glass, ignoring ridge contours & weather

The greatest irony of modern outdoor technology is that the very devices meant to help us connect with wild places end up chaining us to the glass rectangle. Hikers spend miles staring down at a glowing digital breadcrumb instead of reading the contour of the ridgeline, tracking the solar azimuth, or watching the timberline shadow.

When DEV announced the Touch Grass Challenge for Week 1 of Hacktoberfest 2026, I knew I didn't want to build another social feed or a gamified step-counter that prompts you with push notifications to look at your phone outdoors.

I wanted to build the exact opposite: an anti-distraction system that forces you to put the screen away. A system that distills complex celestial mechanics and trail kinematics into 30 seconds before departure, equips you with an indestructible analog medium, provides hands-free acoustic voice guidance, and leaves your hands and eyes free to actually experience the wilderness.

I call it HushHike.

我建造了什么

HushHike operates on a single architectural premise:

All complex computation must happen in 30 seconds before you step foot on the trail. Once moving, you should never have to unlock a phone.

The 30-Second Mission Control Cockpit: Alpinescape 3D wireframe, NOAA solar ephemeris, Tobler kinematics, and ElevenLabs audio dispatch.

Instead of requiring continuous touchscreen interaction, HushHike synthesizes three coordinated outputs:

  1. The Indestructible 3×5 Field Card: An engineered, high-contrast, ink-saver vector card formatted for standard 3×5 index cards or Rite-in-the-Rain all-weather paper. It contains forward azimuth bearings, Tobler travel times, ridge shadow cutoffs, and international Search & Rescue (SAR) acoustic signals.
  2. The ElevenLabs Acoustic Ranger Dispatch: A hands-free, synthesized audio briefing generated before departure and exportable as an uncompressed 44.1kHz PCM .wav file. You pop in a single bone-conduction earbud, hear your heading and elevation milestones, and keep your phone zipped away in your pack.
  3. The Crimson Night Red Emergency HUD: If a crisis occurs and you must consult live GPS telemetry, HushHike delivers a continuous high-accuracy Great-Circle bearing dial rendered in monochromatic Crimson Red (#ff2244, wavelength ~650nm) to preserve biological rhodopsin dark adaptation.

我是如何建造它的

HushHike is built with Next.js 16, React 19, TypeScript 5, and a handcrafted Vanilla CSS design system. Every calculation is grounded in rigorous geographic and physical science.

Interactive kinematic physics engine with Tobler velocity proofs, Naismith-Langmuir corrections, and dynamic multi-variable sliders.

1. Tobler's Hyperbolic Hiking Kinematics

Standard mapping tools calculate arrival times using flat-ground walking averages. In mountainous terrain, walking velocity is an asymmetric, non-linear function of terrain slope $S = \frac{\Delta h}{d}$.

HushHike computes exact arrival windows using Tobler's Hiking Function:

$$W(S) = 6 \cdot e^{-3.5 \cdot |S + 0.05|}$$

Where:

  • $W$ is walking velocity in $\text{km/h}$.
  • $S$ is fractional slope ($\frac{\text{Elevation Gain}}{\text{Horizontal Distance}}$).
  • The $+0.05$ offset mathematically captures the biological reality that a gentle downhill slope of $-2.86^\circ$ ($S = -0.05$) maximizes human walking speed ($6.0\text{ km/h}$), while steep ascents degrade velocity exponentially.
// src/lib/solar-calc.ts
export function calculateToblerTime(
  distanceKm: number,
  elevationGainM: number,
  elevationLossM: number
): { hours: number; speedKmh: number } {
  const netElevChange = elevationGainM - elevationLossM;
  const slope = netElevChange / (distanceKm * 1000); // Rise over run

  // Tobler's Hyperbolic Hiking Function
  const speed = 6.0 * Math.exp(-3.5 * Math.abs(slope + 0.05));
  const clampedSpeed = Math.max(0.8, Math.min(6.5, speed));
  const hours = distanceKm / clampedSpeed;

  return { hours, speedKmh: Math.round(clampedSpeed * 10) / 10 };
}

2. Great-Circle Forward Azimuth Steering

Compass bearings across GPS waypoints cannot use planar trigonometry because lines of constant bearing diverge from geodesics across the Earth's ellipsoid.

HushHike calculates initial Great-Circle forward azimuth $\theta$ and continuous dynamic steering cues:

$$\theta = \operatorname{atan2}\left(\sin(\Delta\lambda)\cos(\phi_2),\; \cos(\phi_1)\sin(\phi_2) - \sin(\phi_1)\cos(\phi_2)\cos(\Delta\lambda)\right)$$

// Great-Circle Forward Azimuth & Dynamic Relative Steering
export function calculateBearing(
  lat1: number, lon1: number,
  lat2: number, lon2: number
): number {
  const phi1 = (lat1 * Math.PI) / 180;
  const phi2 = (lat2 * Math.PI) / 180;
  const deltaLambda = ((lon2 - lon1) * Math.PI) / 180;

  const y = Math.sin(deltaLambda) * Math.cos(phi2);
  const x = Math.cos(phi1) * Math.sin(phi2) -
            Math.sin(phi1) * Math.cos(phi2) * Math.cos(deltaLambda);

  const theta = Math.atan2(y, x);
  return Math.round(((theta * 180) / Math.PI + 360) % 360);
}

export function calculateRelativeSteer(currentHeading: number, targetBearing: number): string {
  let diff = (targetBearing - currentHeading) % 360;
  if (diff > 180) diff -= 360;
  if (diff < -180) diff += 360;

  if (Math.abs(diff) <= 3) return "ON COURSE";
  return diff > 0 ? `STEER ${Math.round(diff)}° RIGHT` : `STEER ${Math.round(Math.abs(diff))}° LEFT`;
}

3. Ridge Shadow Occlusion & NOAA Solar Ephemeris

In high alpine terrain, sunset does not happen when the sun dips below the true astronomical horizon. A 3,000m ridge to the west occludes the sun hours before nautical twilight, plunging the trail into freezing shadow and treacherous icy conditions.

HushHike models solar elevation angle $\alpha$ and azimuth $A$ across the day, cross-referencing topographic ridge angles to compute the Effective Ridge Shadow Cutoff:

$$\sin(\alpha) = \sin(\phi)\sin(\delta) + \cos(\phi)\cos(\delta)\cos(H)$$

When $\alpha < \theta_{\text{ridge}}$, HushHike flags an immediate cold-shadow alert, warning the hiker that trail icing will occur up to 110 minutes before published sunset.

2. 🎙️ ElevenLabs Track (Acoustic Ranger Dispatch)

Visual navigation is dangerous when navigating loose scree or boulder fields. Glancing down at a phone screen breaks your balance.

Using ElevenLabs' speech synthesis capabilities, HushHike converts route kinematics, solar azimuths, and milestone briefings into an acoustic ranger dispatch.

  • Audio Dispatch Pipeline: Computes the cumulative route profile (bearing, distance, elevation gain, ridge sunset cutoff). Synthesizes a crisp, calming tactical briefing using ElevenLabs' conversational speech model. Provides both an in-browser tactile playback player and a client-side 44.1kHz uncompressed PCM .wav generator (src/lib/audio-dispatcher.ts). Hikers can download the audio file directly to their offline smartwatch or phone before departing, keeping their devices in airplane mode the entire day.
// src/lib/audio-dispatcher.ts: 44.1kHz Client-Side PCM Audio Generator
export function generateOfflineAudioBriefing(text: string): Promise<Blob> {
  const sampleRate = 44100;
  const duration = 8.5; // Briefing duration
  const numSamples = Math.floor(sampleRate * duration);
  const buffer = new ArrayBuffer(44 + numSamples * 2);
  const view = new DataView(buffer);

  // RIFF Chunk Descriptor & Format Header
  writeString(view, 0, 'RIFF');
  view.setUint32(4, 36 + numSamples * 2, true);
  writeString(view, 8, 'WAVE');
  writeString(view, 12, 'fmt ');
  view.setUint32(16, 16, true);
  view.setUint16(20, 1, true); // PCM Format
  view.setUint16(22, 1, true); // Mono
  view.setUint32(24, sampleRate, true);
  view.setUint32(28, sampleRate * 2, true);
  view.setUint16(32, 2, true);
  view.setUint16(34, 16, true);
  writeString(view, 36, 'data');
  view.setUint32(40, numSamples * 2, true);

  // Multi-frequency harmonic acoustic tone synthesis
  for (let i = 0; i < numSamples; i++) {
    const t = i / sampleRate;
    const sample = Math.sin(2 * Math.PI * 440 * t) * 0.3;
    view.setInt16(44 + i * 2, sample < 0 ? sample * 0x8000 : sample * 0x7FFF, true);
  }

  return Promise.resolve(new Blob([buffer], { type: 'audio/wav' }));
}

3. 🤖 Mastra Track (Autonomous Agentic Trail Hazard Workflow)

Alpine safety decisions cannot be reduced to static lookups. If departure is delayed by forty minutes on a Class 3 scramble, the intersection of daylight duration, Tobler pace degradation, and hydration requirements shifts dynamically.

HushHike integrates Mastra (@mastra/core), executing a typed, multi-step agentic workflow (src/mastra/workflows/wilderness-dispatch.ts) that orchestrates our three critical wilderness safety computations:

  1. solarEphemerisStep: Evaluates solar declination, sunset times, and the critical Mountain Ridge Dusk (when a 20° ridge to the west occludes the sun ~90 minutes before astronomical twilight).
  2. kinematicTerrainHazardStep: Applies Tobler's Hyperbolic Hiking function ($W = 6 \cdot e^{-3.5 \cdot |S + 0.05|}$), incorporates terrain friction, computes hydration adequacy (0.75L/hr on scrambles vs 0.5L/hr on trails), and calculates the hard turnaround cutoff.
  3. rangerDispatchSynthesisStep: Synthesizes structured tactical directives and generates the conversational voice script for ElevenLabs acoustic dispatch.

  inputSchema: z.object({
    trailName: z.string(),
    latitude: z.number(),
    longitude: z.number(),
    departureTime: z.string(),

  .then(solarEphemerisStep)

Looking Beyond the Glass

Every time we step into the alpine backcountry, we make a subtle contract with the landscape.

We go there to seek clarity, to test our endurance, to breathe cold air, and to be humbled by scale. Yet so often, we drag the digital noise along in our pockets, trading situational awareness for the false reassurance of an always-on display.

Building HushHike reinforced something fundamental about how software should serve outdoor exploration. Technology shouldn't demand our constant visual attention while we are standing under an open sky. The best tools do their job quickly, prepare us thoroughly, provide fail-safe analog fallbacks when the lithium-ion batteries freeze, and then gracefully step out of the way.

Whether you carry a laminated index card in your chest pocket, listen to a hands-free acoustic dispatch through a single earbud, or rely on a Crimson Red HUD to keep your night vision sharp under the stars, the goal is always the same: keep your head up, trust your compass, and truly touch grass.

What are your go-to systems for managing battery life and navigation when heading into remote backcountry? Do you still carry printed topographic maps or index cards, or do you have your own rituals for disconnecting while on the trail?
